summary:
MosaWali - Adaptive Crop Rotation Planning

Developed by Team MosaWali for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026

MosaWali is a NASA-powered agricultural decision-support platform that helps farmers build profitable, water-wise, and climate-resilient four-year crop rotation strategies. Combining NASA Earth observations and multi-decade agroclimatology with soil grids, crop science, Georgian agricultural economics, and farmers' harvest experience, it infers personalized digital field profiles without requiring laboratory soil tests.

The platform evaluates and ranks four-year crop sequences across three farmer-controlled priorities: profitability, water conservation, and soil regeneration. Its Counterfactual Simulator explores how alternative crops would have performed under the same historical weather, while the Climate Stress Lab tests rotations against historical droughts, heat shifts, and extreme seasons.

Unlike static crop planners, MosaWali adapts each season: farmers log actual management and harvests to update field estimates, soil carryover accounts, and remaining rotation years. Its Farm Finance Passport summarizes multi-year cash-flow resilience and NASA-weather harvest consistency to support agricultural lending conversations.

Our mission is to turn single-season guesswork into adaptive, multi-year planning that protects farmers' livelihoods and the land.
details:
MosaWali - Project Details

MosaWali is a bilingual (Georgian/English) agricultural decision-support platform that helps smallholder and medium-scale farmers design profitable, water-wise, and climate-resilient four-year crop rotations. Rather than recommending a single crop in isolation, it combines NASA Earth observations, soil grids, mechanistic crop-water science, Georgian agricultural economics, and farmers' own harvest experience to turn single-season guesswork into adaptive, multi-year planning.

How it works

  • Interactive Field Mapping & Bayesian Profiling: Farmers draw or select their parcel on an interactive satellite map and answer a short sequence of adaptive questions about past crops, harvests, and irrigation. Using two-dimensional Bayesian inference and Shannon information-gain question selection, MosaWali estimates the field's effective Total Available Water Capacity (TAWC) and Fertility Index—giving farmers a calibrated digital field profile even without an expensive laboratory soil test (while incorporating lab results and management details when available).
  • Coupled Crop, Water & Soil Account Simulation: For each candidate crop sequence, a daily agro-hydrological engine computes FAO-56 Penman-Monteith reference evapotranspiration (ET0), runs a two-layer (0–0.5 m and 0.5–1.5 m) daily soil-water balance with SCS curve-number runoff, and tracks season-to-season Soil Account carryover: deep root-zone moisture, mineral and legume-fixed nitrogen (reducing next year's fertilizer expenses), family-specific soilborne disease pressure (Sclerotinia, Take-all, Fusarium), and soil organic matter.
  • Exact Four-Year Multi-Objective Optimization: MosaWall-E evaluates all K4 four-year crop sequences across rolling historical NASA weather windows and identifies Pareto-optimal plans across three farmer-controlled priorities: Profitability (expected net margin in Constant-2025 GEL/ha/yr and worst-decile CVaR 10% bad-year income), Water Conservation (seasonal water deficit in mm/yr), and Soil Regeneration (0–100 Soil Health Index).

Key capabilities

  • Counterfactual Simulator: Replays historical growing seasons with 365-day root-zone water traces so farmers can see how an alternative crop or rotation would have performed financially and hydrologically under the exact weather their field experienced.
  • Climate Stress Lab: Stress-tests strategies against historical droughts, flowering-window heat waves, wet harvests, multi-decade warming shifts (1982–2000 vs. 2001–2025), and mid-century CMIP6 (SSP3-7.0, 2041–2060) yield projections.
  • Adaptive Field Intelligence: After each season, farmers log actual planting, irrigation, inputs, and harvest outcomes. MosaWali updates the field's Bayesian posterior and Soil Account carryover and re-optimizes the remaining years of the rotation.
  • Farm Finance Passport: Translates multi-year rotation economics into structured agro-lending metrics—Debt Service Coverage Ratio (DSCR), monthly working-capital cash-flow curves, bad-year downside coverage, and a NASA-weather harvest consistency check—to support conversations with rural lenders.

Benefits and intended impact

Continuous monoculture (such as back-to-back winter wheat) depletes deep soil moisture, builds root-disease pressure, and leaves farmers exposed when hot springs or dry autumns strike. MosaWali makes multi-year rotation trade-offs visible in plain financial and agronomic terms: higher bad-year income floors, lower synthetic nitrogen bills through timed grain legumes (chickpea, lentil/field pea), healthier soil structure, and printable one-page plans farmers can take to the field or bank.

Our initial deployment targets Georgia, starting with drought-exposed rainfed plains in Kakheti (Shiraki, Gurjaani, Lagodekhi) alongside Kvemo Kartli (Marneuli), Shida Kartli (Gori), and Samegrelo (Abasha)—regions facing rising flowering heat, variable rainfall, and state agroinsurance that excludes drought. Because the core pipeline runs on global NASA, ISRIC, and FAO datasets, MosaWali can expand to new farming regions worldwide by plugging in local crop-price and cost tables.

Technology, tools, and data

NASA Data & Services:

  • NASA POWER Agroclimatology Daily API (MERRA-2 / CERES, 1981–2025): Daily temperature, solar radiation, humidity, wind, surface/root-zone soil wetness, and precipitation.
  • NASA/JAXA GPM IMERG V07 (1998–2025): Independent satellite precipitation used in an automated Pettitt homogeneity gate.
  • NASA SRTM 90 m DEM: Sub-grid terrain elevation for temperature lapse-rate correction (0.0065 °C/m) and mountain-relief confidence grading.
  • NASA SMAP (L3/L4 Soil Moisture) & NASA AppEEARS: Satellite surface and root-zone soil moisture extraction.
  • NASA EOSDIS GIBS (WMTS): Map layers for MODIS 8-Day NDVI, VIIRS True Color, and SMAP soil moisture.


Agronomic, Soil & Economic Data: ISRIC SoilGrids v2 (250 m texture and organic carbon via Saxton-Rawls pedotransfer), FAO & IIASA GAEZ v5 Cloud-Optimized GeoTIFFs (1–9 km agro-ecological suitability, HWSD v2.01 soil constraints, 2020 yields, and CMIP6 SSP3-7.0 projections), FAOSTAT, and National Statistics Office of Georgia (Geostat 2014–2025 regional prices in Constant-2025 GEL).

Software, Languages & Hardware:

Backend: Python 3.12, FastAPI, NumPy, Pydantic, HTTPX, scikit-learn, Pytest, and a custom pure-Python HTTP Range Cloud-Optimized GeoTIFF reader.

Frontend: TypeScript, Next.js 15, React 19, Tailwind CSS v4, MapLibre GL JS, TerraDraw, Turf.js, Apache ECharts, and next-intl (ka/en).

Hardware & Deployment: Runs on standard laptops, tablets, and smartphones with pre-cached regional site packs for fast response in low-connectivity rural areas.

Creativity and factors considered

Our core innovation is connecting spaceborne Earth observations, farmer memory, stateful soil accounting, and rural finance in one closed-loop system—turning a farmer's recollection of past harvests into a virtual soil sensor, optimizing four-year sequences rather than isolated single crops, and translating climate resilience into bank-ready financial metrics.

Our team designed strictly around scientific honesty and real-world farming constraints:

  • Screening satellite artefacts before advising farmers: At Shiraki (Kakheti), our Pettitt change-point test detected a pre-2003 step shift in reanalysis precipitation (313 mm vs. 555 mm, p=2.2×10^−5) not corroborated by GPM IMERG (p=0.56). MosaWali automatically restricts Shiraki rainfall simulations to homogeneous 2003–2025 windows rather than feeding distorted rainfall trends into farm plans.
  • Correcting coarse climate grids for Caucasus terrain: Where 0.5° climate cells span steep mountain-to-valley relief, SRTM 90 m elevation adjusts field temperatures and flags low spatial confidence above 500 m elevation difference.
  • Machine-learning honesty gate: We benchmarked a Leave-One-Year-Out Ridge regression residual model on 639 historical Georgian yield records (1992–2025), enforcing a strict gate where ML activates at runtime only if out-of-sample error beats the physics model alone, preventing overfitted predictions.
  • Local usability & transparency: Built in Georgian and English with high-contrast, plain-language summaries, one-page A4 printouts, explicit provenance flags distinguishing verified Geostat/tariff figures from placeholder contractor quotes, and credit rules aligned with Georgia's 2026 agricultural lending and drought-insurance realities.
